props.title: The Great Race
props.initialSlug: Epic cross-continental race leads to slapstick chaos

sections.content: The Great Race (1965) stands as Blake Edwards' magnificent love letter to slapstick comedy and early automotive adventures. This lavish $12 million production (enormous for its time) pairs Tony Curtis's immaculate "The Great Leslie" against Jack Lemmon's mustache-twirling Professor Fate in a New York to Paris auto race. The film deliberately channels the spirit of early silent comedies, particularly those of Laurel and Hardy, while amplifying the scale to epic proportions. Like It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World (1963), it represents the apex of big-budget comedy spectacle in the 1960s, featuring elaborate stunts, massive pie fights, and set pieces that would influence later works like Those Magnificent Men in Their Flying Machines (1965) and Around the World in 80 Days (1956).

sections.content: The film's influence on automotive-themed comedies cannot be overstated. Its DNA can be found in everything from The Cannonball Run (1981) to Rat Race (2001). Director Blake Edwards, fresh off his success with The Pink Panther (1963), brought his signature blend of sophisticated comedy and physical humor to the production. The film's massive pie fight sequence took 5 days to shoot and used over 4,000 pies, setting a record at the time and influencing countless future food fights in cinema, including the famous cafeteria scene in Animal House (1978).

Natalie Wood's portrayal of suffragette reporter Maggie DuBois adds a progressive element that was ahead of its time, challenging gender roles while maintaining the film's comedic tone. The movie's stunning production design won an Academy Award, with its meticulous recreation of period automobiles and elaborate European locations. The influence of The Great Race extends to modern films like The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014), which shares its love of elaborate chases and color-coded character design. sections.content: The film's technical achievements set new standards for comedy productions. Cinematographer Russell Harlan, who had worked on To Kill a Mockingbird (1962), brought a sophisticated visual style that elevated the slapstick material. The film's use of the Ultra Panavision 70 widescreen format allowed for spectacular vistas and complex action sequences that would influence later road movies like Mad Max (1979) and Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981).
